questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Locate the foci of an ellipse from its semi-axes
questions.stem: Clinical note 4612 records an ellipse used to model a treatment zone, with a semi-axis of 5 cm and a semi-axis of 4 cm. Where are its foci?

options.text: At plus and minus 3 cm from the centre, since c squared equals a squared minus b squared.
At plus and minus 4 cm from the centre, since the smaller semi-axis sets the focal distance.
options.misconception: uses the minor semi-axis as the focal distance

options.text: At plus and minus 5 cm from the centre, since the larger semi-axis sets the focal distance.
options.misconception: uses the major semi-axis as the focal distance

options.text: At plus and minus 9 cm from the centre, since the focal distance is the sum of the semi-axes.
options.misconception: adds the semi-axes to get the focal distance

questions.explanation: For an ellipse the focal distance satisfies c squared equals a squared minus b squared, which is 25 minus 16, so c equals 3. The foci therefore sit 3 cm from the centre along the major axis.
questions.hint: Use c squared equals a squared minus b squared.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the eccentricity of an ellipse
questions.stem: Clinical note 4613 gives a treatment ellipse with a of 5 cm and b of 4 cm. What is its eccentricity, to two decimals?
questions.explanation: The focal distance is the square root of 25 minus 16, which is 3, and the eccentricity is c over a, which is 3 over 5, giving 0.60. Every ellipse has an eccentricity below one.
questions.hint: Compute c first, then divide by a.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cross term forces a rotation
questions.stem: Clinical note 4614 asks why a conic whose cross term is not zero must be rotated before its standard form can be read off.

options.text: Because the cross term always records a translation of the centre away from the origin.
options.misconception: attributes the cross term to a shift of the centre

options.text: Because the cross term shows the axes are tilted, so the conic must be turned to align them.
Because the cross term changes the value of the eccentricity of the conic.
options.misconception: believes the cross term alters the eccentricity

options.text: Because a conic with a cross term has no centre and cannot be centred at all.
options.misconception: denies that such conics can have a centre

questions.explanation: A nonzero cross term means the conic is tilted relative to the coordinate axes, so it must be rotated to reveal its principal axes. It describes orientation, not position.
questions.hint: The cross term records the tilt of the axes.

questions.stem: Clinical note 4615 models a beam profile with y squared equals 8x. What is the distance from the vertex to the focus in units?
questions.explanation: A parabola in the form y squared equals 4px has its focus p units from the vertex, so comparing 4p with 8 gives p equal to 2. The directrix then sits the same distance on the other side.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the area of an ellipse from its semi-axes
questions.stem: Clinical note 4616 shows an ellipse centred at the origin with semi-axes 6 cm and 2 cm. What is its area in square centimetres?

options.text: 37.7, because the area is the sum of the two semi-axes times pi.
options.misconception: adds the semi-axes instead of multiplying them

options.text: 18.85, because the area is half the product of the semi-axes times pi.
options.misconception: halves the area without a reason

options.text: 37.7, because the area of an ellipse is pi times a times b.
12, because the area is the product of the two semi-axes alone.
options.misconception: drops the pi factor from the area formula

questions.explanation: The area of an ellipse is pi times the product of the two semi-axes, so pi times 6 times 2 gives about 37.70 square centimetres. Halving that figure would describe something smaller than the ellipse.
questions.hint: Ellipse area is pi a b.

questions.learningObjective: Find the error in a claim that no rotation is needed
questions.stem: Clinical note 4617 reviews a conic written as x squared plus 2xy plus 3y squared equals 1 and claims the axes need no rotation. What is wrong?

options.text: The xy term shows the conic is tilted, so a rotation is needed before reading parameters.
The claim is wrong only if the constant on the right hand side is changed.
options.misconception: invents a condition about the constant term

options.text: The claim is wrong, because a conic with an xy term has no centre.
options.misconception: denies that a tilted conic can have a centre

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the equation already contains only squared terms.
options.misconception: thinks squared terms alone rule out a tilt

questions.explanation: The xy term means the quadratic part is not aligned with the axes, so the conic is tilted and must be rotated before its parameters can be read. The constant term does not affect the tilt.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the directrices of an ellipse relative to its foci
questions.stem: Clinical note 4618 asks where the directrices of an ellipse sit relative to its foci and its curve.

options.text: They lie inside the ellipse, between the two foci.
options.misconception: places the directrices inside the ellipse

options.text: They pass through the foci, one line through each focus.
options.misconception: confuses the directrices with lines through the foci

options.text: They are tangent to the ellipse at the ends of the minor axis.
options.misconception: places the directrices as tangents at the minor axis ends

options.text: They lie outside the ellipse, farther from the centre than the foci.

questions.explanation: Each directrix of an ellipse is a line at a distance of a over e from the centre, which exceeds a and so places it outside the curve, beyond the foci. They are not tangents.
questions.hint: Compare a over e with the semi-axis a.

questions.explanation: The asymptotes of this hyperbola are y equals plus or minus 4 over 3 times x, so the slope is 1.3333. The ratio of the two semi-axes gives the tilt of the asymptotes.
questions.hint: Divide b by a for the asymptote slope.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why translation preserves the shape of an ellipse

options.text: Because the shift changes the coefficients but leaves the semi-axes alone.
options.misconception: claims the shift alters the coefficients

options.text: Because translating an ellipse turns it into a hyperbola.
options.misconception: claims translation changes the conic family

options.text: Because a translation moves the centre without changing the semi-axes or the shape.
Because the semi-axes are always measured from the origin after a shift.
options.misconception: believes the semi-axes are measured from the origin

questions.explanation: A translation slides the whole curve to a new centre without resizing it, so the semi-axes and the eccentricity stay the same. Only the position of the centre changes.

questions.explanation: The focal distance satisfies c squared equals 25 plus 144, which is 169, so c equals 13. The eccentricity is c over a, which is 13 over 5, giving 2.6, and a hyperbola always exceeds one.

questions.learningObjective: Find the distance from a parabola vertex to its directrix
questions.stem: Clinical note 4622 shows the parabola y squared equals 12x with its vertex at the origin. What is the distance from the vertex to the directrix?

options.text: 12 units, because the coefficient of x squared is the distance to the directrix.
options.misconception: confuses the equation coefficient with the focal distance

options.text: 3 units, because 4p equals 12 gives p equals 3, and the directrix sits p to the left.
1 unit, because every parabola has its directrix one unit from the vertex.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed one-unit distance for every parabola

options.text: 6 units, because the coefficient 12 should be halved before anything else.
options.misconception: halves the coefficient without using the standard form

questions.learningObjective: Find the error in a claim about a tilted conic
questions.stem: Clinical note 4623 reviews an equation x squared plus 2xy plus 3y squared equals 1 that was claimed to describe a circle. What is wrong?

options.text: The xy term shows the conic is tilted, so the curve is an ellipse rather than a circle.

options.misconception: suggests changing the constant would produce a circle

options.text: The equation is wrong because a circle cannot contain an xy term in any form.
options.misconception: denies that a tilted ellipse can carry an xy term

questions.explanation: The xy term shows the quadratic part is not equal in both directions, so the curve is a tilted ellipse rather than a circle. A circle needs no cross term.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the foci of a translated ellipse
questions.stem: Clinical note 4624 gives the curve (x minus 3) squared over 25 plus (y plus 1) squared over 16 equals 1. Where are its two foci?

options.text: At (6,-1) and (0,-1), since c equals 3 and the centre is (3,-1).
At (8,-1) and (-2,-1), since the semi-major axis sets the focal distance.
options.misconception: uses the semi-major axis as the focal distance

options.text: At (5,0) and (-5,0), since the foci always sit on the horizontal axis.
options.misconception: ignores the translation when placing the foci

options.text: At (3,4) and (3,-4), since the centre determines the foci vertically.
options.misconception: puts the foci on the vertical axis through the centre

questions.explanation: The centre is (3,-1) and the focal distance is the square root of 25 minus 16, which is 3, so the foci lie 3 units left and right of the centre. Translation moves the foci with the curve.

questions.stem: Clinical note 4625 gives an ellipse with a of 4 cm and b of 2 cm. What is its eccentricity to three decimals?
questions.explanation: The focal distance is the square root of 16 minus 4, which is the square root of 12, about 3.46410. Dividing by a gives the eccentricity 0.866, which is below one as an ellipse requires.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Determine the direction of a rotation from coefficients
questions.stem: Clinical note 4626 shows a tilted conic whose quadratic form is 3x squared plus 2xy plus y squared. In which direction are the axes rotated?

options.text: Clockwise, because the coefficient on x squared is larger than the one on y squared.
options.misconception: guesses the direction from one squared coefficient

options.text: Counterclockwise, because B over A minus C is positive, so the angle is positive.
Clockwise, because the cross term coefficient is positive.
options.misconception: reads the sign of the cross term as the sign of the angle

options.text: There is no rotation, because both squared terms are present.
options.misconception: believes squared terms rule out any rotation

questions.explanation: The tangent of twice the rotation angle equals B over A minus C, which is 2 over 3 minus 1, a positive value, so the rotation is counterclockwise. The signs alone do not decide it.
questions.hint: Compute B over A minus C first.

options.misconception: claims the smaller semi-axis sets the major axis

options.text: The major axis is the denominator of the term with the negative coefficient.
options.misconception: invents a rule about negative coefficients

options.text: The larger denominator gives the major axis, since the denominators are squared semi-axes.

questions.explanation: Each denominator is the square of a semi-axis, so the larger denominator gives the larger semi-axis and hence the major axis. The denominators themselves are not the axis lengths.

questions.learningObjective: Find the error in a reported rotation angle
questions.stem: Clinical note 4629 gives a tilted conic 3x squared plus 4xy plus 5y squared equals 1 and reports a rotation angle of 63.43 degrees. What went wrong?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the arctangent gives the rotation angle directly.
options.misconception: accepts the arctangent value as the angle

options.text: The angle should be 15.86 degrees, since the arctangent must be divided by four.
options.misconception: divides the arctangent by the wrong amount

options.text: The angle should be 126.87 degrees, since the arctangent must be doubled.
options.misconception: doubles the arctangent value instead of halving it

options.text: The arctangent gives twice the angle, so the rotation is about 31.72 degrees.

questions.explanation: The tangent of twice the angle equals 4 over 3 minus 5, which is negative 2, so twice the angle is negative 63.43 degrees and the tilt is 31.72. The arctangent is twice the angle.
questions.hint: The formula returns twice the angle.

options.misconception: adds the semi-axes to get the focal distance

options.text: At (5,0) and (-5,0), since c squared equals 16 plus 9, which is 25.
At (3,0) and (-3,0), since the conjugate semi-axis sets the focal distance.

options.text: At (4,0) and (-4,0), since the vertices sit 4 units from the centre.
options.misconception: confuses the vertices with the foci

questions.explanation: For a hyperbola c squared equals a squared plus b squared, which is 16 plus 9, so c equals 5 and the foci sit at plus and minus 5 on the transverse axis. The vertices are closer in.

options.text: Because only one adjustment is ever needed, whichever feature the equation carries.
options.misconception: believes one adjustment always suffices

questions.explanation: The right directrix sits at x equal to 25 over 3, about 8.3333, and the right focus is at x equal to 3. The gap between them is 8.3333 minus 3, which is 5.3333, that is 16 over 3.

questions.stem: Clinical note 4644 shows the ellipse written as (x minus 2) squared over 9 plus (y plus 4) squared over 4 equals 1. Where is its centre?

options.misconception: reads the bracket signs as the centre coordinates

options.text: At (0,0), because the centre of a shifted ellipse stays at the origin.
